transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-13 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Sofia (HarborGrid Head of ML), Raj (HarborGrid Platform), Lindsey (HarborGrid SRE), Paul (Product)

Summary (auto-generated): Kickoff to scope POC focused on traffic geometry, token mix and burst absorption. Customer provided high-level KPIs: p99 tail latency target 500ms for 256-token generates, steady-state QPS ~150 with intermittent bursts to 1.2k for 45-120s. Redwood recommended replay benchmark + three model configs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood, i'll kick us off. Uh quick round of intros?
[00:08] Sofia: yeah hi i'm sofia head of ml at HarborGrid. we run the QA / summarization pipeline for customer support.
[00:14] Raj: raj here, platform eng, and i'm focused on reliability and cost.
[00:17] Lindsey: lindsey, sre — i'll own the operability side.
[00:21] Diego: diego, senior solutions eng at Redwood — i'll be driving the benchmark harness and replay.
[00:25] Maya: great. quick context from HarborGrid: sofia, can you remind us of the current traffic shape? steady qps and burst behavior?
[00:33] Sofia: yeah so steady is around 120 to 170 eq qps during the day, but we have three main burst patterns — a short rapid fan-out when a batch job kicks off in the morning that can hit about 900 to 1.2k QPS for about 60 to 90 seconds, and then a slower midnight index job that runs for 20 minutes hitting 400 qps, and occasional long tails when a big customer runs a report up to 6k tokens per request. We care a lot about p99 for the interactive path.
[01:05] Maya: ok cool. what's the typical concurrency from your service side? connection pools?
[01:10] Raj: our app holds about 200 concurrent HTTP connections in the busiest nodes; we scale pods horizontally but the lambda of concurrency is effectively capped by DB workers too — so we need predictable headroom.
[01:21] Lindsey: we also need graceful degradation — if the model is slower we prefer a reduced-quality fallback or truncated response over a complete timeout.
[01:29] Diego: noted. two quick clarifying questions about tokens: what's the input token distribution and output length on average?
[01:35] Sofia: avg input is small — like 12 to 25 tokens for query plus a 40–120 token system context, so total input median around 60. Output median is around 90 tokens, but 10% of requests go long (300–4k tokens) for report generation.
[01:52] Maya: perfect. that helps. so our POC plan: replay the 48h trace you provide, run three model configurations (baseline fp16, int8 quant, and a compact distilled variant), and measure median/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, and cost per million tokens. We'll also capture tail-latency under burst.
[02:10] Paul: timeline? how long will this take?
[02:13] Maya: we propose a 4-week pilot. week1 - trace ingestion and replay harness setup, week2 - run benchmarks across three configs (both hosted and dedicated sim), week3 - analyze results and run tuning (batching, prefix cache timeouts), week4 - run final tuned benchmark and deliver recommendation + pilot contract.
[02:34] Raj: on dedicated vs hosted — for us security/compliance matters, but we want to see cost/lateny tradeoffs first. can you simulate VPC network egress?
[02:43] Diego: yes we can run the benchmarks from our hosted fleet and also spin up a private sim environment that approximates VPC egress latency. we will include 50ms added network RTT in the sim to match your edge.
[02:53] Lindsey: what about caching — the prefix cache you mentioned in docs, will that help the p99?
[02:58] Diego: prefix caching/KV cache helps a lot for repeat conversational patterns. for one-off long reports it's less effective. we'll capture cache hit rate in the replay metrics and show delta in both latency and token cost.
[03:10] Sofia: our concern is bursts — do you have burst absorption knobs?
[03:13] Maya: yes, we have autoscaling and burst credits on Redwood Dedicated and you can configure graceful fallback routing to a smaller model if capacity strained. For the POC we'll test fallback scenarios: cold fallback to compact model, and progressive prefix-truncate to reduce output tokens.
[03:29] Diego: for benchmarks we'll instrument request-level telemetry: queue time, service time, kv cache hit, model execution time, tokens in/out, and cost per call. we'll also produce QPS heatmaps and a burst replay where we superimpose your 60–90s morning spike.
[03:45] Raj: any expected per-call overhead in your hosted env? we have microservices that add 25–50ms before hitting model endpoint.
[03:52] Diego: we'll parameterize that in the harness. good to have your exact network numbers.
[03:56] Sofia: what about tokenization differences across models — does quantization change token counts?
[04:01] Diego: tokenization is model-dependent but not changed by quantization. however, output length can vary slightly with different model variants so we'll normalize comparisons by forcing identical decoding constraints (stop tokens, max tokens).
[04:15] Maya: success criteria check — sofia can you confirm the minimal bar? i heard p99 < 500ms for up to 256 output tokens on interactive path and max acceptable cost per 1M tokens is $XX (placeholder until pricing shared).
[04:28] Sofia: yes p99 < 500ms is our sweet spot; if that can't be met we'd accept a p99 < 800ms with fallback. Cost target we'll share as a number in the deck.
[04:36] Paul: what about SLOs under burst — do you define degraded SLOs?
[04:40] Maya: we typically define primary SLO for steady 95th/median and a secondary degraded SLO for burst windows. We'll provide a playback report that shows SLO compliance under repeated burst shapes.
[04:50] Lindsey: security items — we'll need SOC2 summary and SAML SSO flow. also encryption in flight and at rest — KMS details for private deployment.
[04:59] Maya: we'll include SOC2 + VPC onboarding checklist, and Diego will follow up with a KMS integration note.
[05:05] Diego: action item for me is to prepare the replay harness repo and an example runbook. i'll also add optional flags for prefix cache TTL and dynamic batching sizes so we can tune.
[05:16] Raj: for the replay, do you need de-identified payloads or full raw logs?
[05:20] Sofia: we can provide de-identified traces and a mapping file. we'll also provide a small sample of full raw requests to validate tokenization.
[05:28] Maya: perfect. on measurement cadence — we'll run each config for 30 minutes steady-state, then run a 2-minute head-of-burst stress and a 60–90s replay of the morning spike three times to get p99s.
[05:42] Diego: recommended metrics to collect: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, model GPU ms per token, mem usage, cache hit rate, failed calls, and cost-per-token. we'll output a spreadsheet matching these columns.
[05:56] Sofia: sounds good. can you also include concurrency and inflight-requests histogram, we want to know queue-length distribution.
[06:01] Diego: yes. we'll include queue latency histograms and a qps vs p99 curve.
[06:06] Maya: last thing — success gates for moving to a production pilot: (1) replay shows p99 < 500ms for 80% of steady windows, (2) cost per 1M tokens within target, (3) defined fallback behavior that meets degraded SLO.
[06:21] Paul: agreed.
[06:22] Maya: ok let's recap next steps and owners — sofia will send the traces by Oct 19, diego will share harness and initial runbook by Oct 22, maya will send the pricing slide and SOC2/VPC checklist by Oct 16, and we'll schedule the benchmark window for week of Oct 26.
[06:40] Sofia: thanks everyone, excited to see the numbers.
[06:43] Maya: thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the repo link.

End transcript.
